lines.text: This is the exact difference between Git and GitHub.
Git is a tool on your laptop. It remembers every version of your code.
GitHub is a website. It keeps that history online, so a whole team can work on it.
Let's follow one line of code, from your laptop, all the way to live.
Step one. The mess. Without Git, your folder looks like this. Final. Final two. Really final. Which one actually works?
Step two. Commit. With Git, you take a snapshot of your whole project. Like a save point in a game.
Each save gets a message, and a unique ID, forty characters long. Break something later? Jump back to any save.
That snapshot is called a commit. Git was built in two thousand five, by the team behind Linux.
Step three. Branch. Want to try a risky idea, without breaking what works? Make a branch. A safe parallel copy.
And it's cheap. A new branch is just a tiny file, forty one bytes, pointing at a commit.
Step four. GitHub. So far, everything lives on your laptop. Spill coffee on it, and your history's gone.
So you push it to GitHub. Now there's a copy online, and your teammates can pull it down.
Over a hundred and eighty million developers build there.
But now ten people can change the same code. What stops them from wrecking it?
Quick thing. Git, GitHub and GitHub Actions is a free course. You can learn it on Teyro.
Okay. Back to the code.
Step five. Pull request. You don't change the main code directly. You ask first.
A pull request says: here's my branch, please check it. A teammate reviews it, leaves comments, then merges it in.
And here's the trap every beginner hits. Two people edit the same line.
Git can't guess who's right, so it stops and asks you. That's a merge conflict.
It looks scary. It isn't. You pick the line you want, delete the markers, and commit again.
Step seven. GitHub Actions. Now the best part. Every time you push, a robot wakes up on GitHub's servers.
It installs your project, runs your tests, and if everything passes, puts it live.
You write the steps once, in a small file, in a folder called dot github, slash workflows.
Engineers call this CI CD. Test everything. Ship automatically.
So here's our one line of code. You fix a typo. Commit. Push. Open a pull request. The robot tests it. A teammate approves. And it's live.
To be fair, you don't need all of this on day one. Start with commits. The rest comes fast.
So. Git remembers your code. GitHub shares it. Branches keep it safe. Pull requests get it reviewed. Actions test it and ship it.
Git saves your code. GitHub shares it. That's the difference.
